newsitem.title: POLAND: New Polish party taps pensioner power at election.
newsitem.headline: New Polish party taps pensioner power at election.

text.p: A new party aiming to champion Poland's huge army of pensioners flexed its muscles on Tuesday by declaring it would fight this year's parliamentary polls by itself and win at least eight percent of the vote.

The Pensioners' Party (KPEiR), created in 1994 and grouping some 23,000 members, is scoring nearly as well as major established opposition parties in opinion polls and showing that pensioner power is a force to be reckoned with.

Party chiefs told a news conference they wanted to ensure retired Poles had a share in the country's economic growth and needed their own representatives to watch over work on a crucial reform of the social security system to ensure it did not harm their interests.
"We are not a party of demands...By taking care of our own circles' interest we only want a share that would reflect the country's economic growth," party adviser Zdzislaw Kruzel said.

Kruzel said that in recent years pension increases had lagged behind economic growth, which was nearly six percent last year, because social security reform had so far involved only curbs on the growth of pensions and benefits.

The government, which says public finances will collapse after 2004 unless the current pay-as-you-go pension system is reformed, has cut the growth of pensions by pegging it to prices rather than to average wage rises as was previously the case.
An average Polish pension is now 608 zlotys ($200), or some 60 percent of the national average wage.
Party leader Stanislaw Tarka said he was counting on at least eight percent of the vote in the elections, which are due around September.

He suggested the party could enter a government coalition with either of the parties forecast to do well in the ballot -- the co-ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) or the opposition right-leaning Solidarity Electoral Action (AWS).
"We will go to the elections by ourselves...and we will talk about any coalition only after the elections," Tarka said.

Several recent polls have suggested the Pensioners' Party had support of between five and eight percent, showing it might be one of seven parties getting more than the five percent of the vote needed to enter parliament.
This support could grow if the party can attract more of the nine million Poles collecting pensions or disability benefits.
These pensioners form a powerful group among the 39 million population -- one which can perhaps be stirred into action by fears social security reform could cut their incomes.
In the last elections in 1993, eight percent support translated into 41 seats in the 460-strong lower house of parliament, while five percent of the votes returned 22 seats.

Recent polls have indicated that both the ex-communists and the Solidarity alliance -- each with more than 20 percent support which could give them well above 120 seats -- will need to join forces with smaller parties to form a government.
Tarka said that the Pensioners' Party, which he called a centrist group, was ready for a coalition only if its partner showed understanding for its social and economic programme.

The party's economic adviser Edward Zdrojowy said, without giving details, that the group backed continued economic growth, measures to cut unemployment, now at 13 percent, stimulation of exports and tax incentives for investors.
He said the Polish economy needed foreign investment but his party was in favour of privatising firms only by selling stakes to passive investors and not to strategic ones.
